scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Pantomime traditions of imitating mannequins and mechanical figures date back to the 1920s, mirroring the rise of the industrial machine age.

In the late 1960s, street mime Robert Shields performed mechanical man illusions at the Hollywood Wax Museum in Los Angeles, inspiring urban dancers to integrate rigid isolations into soul and funk environments.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally staged as theatrical street mime and later shared as a popular novelty social dance at parties, clubs, and television specials.
The movement reflects artistic fascination with automation, robotics, and industrial technology, translating mechanical rigidity into athletic urban expression.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dancer holds a rigid, upright posture and isolates individual limbs, rotating or shifting joints along strict geometric planes.
Each motion begins and ends with a dimestop—a sudden, absolute freeze—or a locking pause that gives the illusion of mechanical gears engaging and halting.
Practitioners may add muscular pops on the rhythmic beat while preserving a stiff, automated silhouette.
Watch for dimestop, pop on beat.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The robot is danced to music with distinct, steady rhythms, particularly funk, soul, electrofunk, and robo trance.
Performers also dance to songs themed around robotics, such as Styx's 'Mr. Roboto', or perform a cappella, generating their own robotic motor sound effects, clicks, and beatbox percussion.
Listen for the synthesizer, drum machine, electric bass, electric guitar.
The pulse is 4/4.

Distinct, highly regular rhythmic pulses driven by heavy bass lines, crisp snare hits, and electric synthesizer accents. Music often incorporates electrofunk grooves or sparse funk breaks where physical stops align with sudden percussive strikes and simulated machine clicks.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Historically performed in everyday street clothes, social party attire, or formal stage costumes worn by musical groups on television broadcasts.
Performers also dance in theatrical robot outfits or character costumes, such as in music videos or street theatre outside tourist venues like the Hollywood Wax Museum.
The dance occurs in street squares, social dance clubs, television studios, and stage arenas.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Robert Shields, Charles 'Robot' Washington, Robot Ann, Michael Jackson, Damita Jo Freeman, Don Campbell, James Brown, and James Higgins (Skeeter Rabbit).
Social couple dancing in Californian funk clubs; solo street theatre pantomime in Los Angeles; synchronised ensemble routines developed internationally for stage and world record events.

Evolved from early 20th-century theatrical mime, puppeting, and mechanical doll pantomime; merged into African American funk and soul social dancing in the late 1960s; later cross-pollinated with popping and locking.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: robot is variant of popping: Poppers regularly incorporate the robot into routines by punctuating automaton illusions with muscular pops.
robot is influence of locking: Robot movements routinely use locking halts to signal the starting and stopping of mechanical motors.
robot is influence of puppeting: Shares historical lineage with jazz-era pantomime where dancers mimicked wind-up musical box dolls.

scenes.title: Welcome
narration: Chapter 1 — First steps. Today: Master the abrupt start-stop mechanic in isolation..
Level: Level 1: The Dimestop. Difficulty of the dance overall: intermediate.
Your instructor: A seasoned street dance historian and popper who teaches with surgical geometric precision and historical clarity.
on_screen: Instructor front view, name of the chapter, the three things you will learn

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Rigid, upright posture held throughout the performance, with controlled muscle tone to maintain the illusion of mechanical parts.
Segmented arm extensions and angular elbow bends that move independently and freeze with abrupt dimestops.
Isolated torso tilts and rotational freezes, avoiding fluid pelvic rolling or natural body waves.
on_screen: Instructor front then side view; freeze-frame on posture

scenes.title: Count and rhythm
narration: Count: 1-2-3-4-5-6. The meter is 4/4.
Rhythm pattern: Heavy, distinct syncopated beat with sharp accents suitable for robotic stops..
Clap it first, then step it in place.
on_screen: Counts on screen, flashing on the beat
Metronome — tempo MISSING, use a slow comfortable pulse

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Assume a rigid, upright neutral stance with feet planted and core engaged.
Step 2: Initiate a single-limb isolation along an angular plane, moving at a constant rate.
Footwork from the sources: Stilted, stepped foot placements that start and halt sharply on rigid angles without fluid weight shifts.
Drill: Extend one forearm outward along a flat plane and halt abruptly on count 1.
on_screen: Instructor front view, then back view (student's perspective); repetitions per step: about 2
Counts on screen

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: Execute a dimestop, abruptly freezing the limb to simulate a motor shutting down.
Step 4: Optionally add a rhythmic pop on the musical pulse while preserving the rigid silhouette.
Drill: Hold the arm motionless for count 2, maintaining rigid tension.
on_screen: Instructor front and back view; slow, then half tempo

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Step A, then Step B, without stopping. Slow first.
Now half tempo. Now full tempo.
Mirror: the instructor faces you and mirrors, so your right is your right.
Drill: Rotate the wrist 90 degrees on count 3 and dimestop instantly on count 4.
on_screen: Split screen: front view / back view
Tempo label changes: slow → half → full

scenes.title: Common mistakes and what to avoid
narration: Avoid fluid, continuous body rolls or casual slouching, which instantly break the illusion of an automaton.
on_screen: Side-by-side: wrong / right
